title: the dice game
hook: before the first throw, Yudhishthira calls the game deceit, Shakuni dares him, and he plays anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday the blind king had a hall built for the game, and sent Vidura, who had warned against it, to carry the invitation. Let a worry change one thing.

The new hall is ready, and Yudhishthira has come. The guests are seated, the cloth is spread, and the dice are out. Before anyone throws, there's a conversation, and it's easy to hurry past it on the way to the drama. Don't. Everything that follows is already folded inside it. Yudhishthira says plainly what he thinks of this kind of game. Shakuni answers him, and the answer has a hook in it. And a choice gets made in the open, before the elders have even taken their seats.
screen: `THE BOARD IS SET.` → `A CONVERSATION FIRST.` → `A CHOICE MADE IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shakuni opens: the hall is full; it's time to play. Yudhishthira doesn't pretend. Gambling of this kind is deceit, he says; there's no warrior's courage in it. Don't beat us by crooked means. Shakuni's answer is clever. Every contest is one person knowing more than another. A skilled player beats an unskilled one, a learned person beats one who isn't, and nobody calls that cheating. Then the sting: if you're afraid, don't play. Yudhishthira's reply is the hinge of the whole episode. Called to play, I don't turn back; that's my vow. And fate rules everyone. So he asks who he'll be playing against. Duryodhana answers: I'll put up the wealth, and my uncle Shakuni will throw for me. Yudhishthira sees the problem at once. One man playing with another's stake seems to him against the rules. But if that's how they want it, let it begin. In a few lines, he named the danger and the unfairness, was told that refusing would look like fear, and walked forward anyway, holding a vow and a belief about fate. Some readers call that integrity. Others call it pride. The poem gives both something to hold. The elders come in and take their seats, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vidura among them, with heavy hearts, the poem says. Yudhishthira puts down his first stake, a costly pearl set in gold. Shakuni throws. And he wins.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA: THIS GAME IS DECEIT.` · `SHAKUNI: IF YOU'RE AFRAID, DON'T PLAY.` · `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.` · `ONE MAN THROWS FOR ANOTHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST STAKE: A PEARL SET IN GOLD.`

segments.voice: Say quietly to yourself a rule you keep and are a little proud of: I always finish what I start, I never say no to family, I don't back down. Then ask it one question: has it ever walked you somewhere you'd already said out loud was a mistake? Don't drop it or defend it; hold it up to the light for a few breaths, bringing it into your prayer if you pray, or simply letting the breath carry it if not.
Vrata, a vow that won't let him turn back. Before the first throw, a warning spoken aloud, a dare to answer it, and this vow that walks a king to the board.
Your line: ask whose voice that is. A vow can hold you up, or walk you to the board. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The dice scene is retold in homes, on stage and on screen, and the talk before the first throw is a place where readers and listeners stop to argue about Yudhishthira's choice.

chat.says: Yudhishthira knew the game was crooked. Why did he still sit down to play?
options: He'd vowed never to turn back when called to play, and believed fate rules everyone.
Duryodhana agreed to throw the dice himself, which seemed fair enough.
Vidura had told him the game would be fair and safe to play.
chat.meaning: Called to play, I don't turn back; that's my vow, he says, and fate rules everyone. He named the unfairness and walked forward anyway.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Yudhishthira calls deceitful gambling sinful and without kshatriya prowess; Shakuni's reply that a skilled player beating an unskilled one is not called deceit, and 'if you are afraid, desist'; Yudhishthira's 'summoned, I do not withdraw' as his vow, with fate all-powerful.
Confirm Yudhishthira's objection that playing through another's agency seems contrary to rule.
Confirm the elders who enter (Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Vidura) and the phrase about cheerless or heavy hearts.
Confirm the first stake: Ganguli has a costly pearl set in gold.
Original: vrata is offered as the general word for a vow; the script does not claim this word appears in the Sanskrit here. A Keeper may prefer null.
